research_concepts: defensive suppression of opponent H2-H1 change
regression to the mean in H1->H2 change
methodological_questions: Does a team's defensive effect on opponents' H2-H1 change persist across odd/even games and across consecutive seasons after removing regression to the mean?
How much true between-team variance exists relative to sampling noise at 120 team-seasons?
How should opponent H1 level, opponent quality, score state, garbage time and rest be controlled?
Is there a mechanical dependence of H2-H1 change on H1 level that would create or hide a team effect?

historical_evidence.finding: First-half reliance on a play type predicting H2 suppression: matched ATT did not survive BH adjustment (PNR ATT=+0.0313, BH_p=0.0658, WEAK; others NULL). Predictive lift over a mean-reversion baseline was +0.039 (0.550 vs 0.511). The record states the bulk of H2 suppression is RTM. n=8873 team-games.

Variance of H1->H2 PPP collapse: H1 PPP alone (RTM) explains 32.9% of variance and is 95% of the explained part. Usage, process/shot-zone, lineup and context add about 1.7 pp in total. 65.4% is unexplained, described as idiosyncratic noise from small per-half n. n=40963 cells; verdict null, high confidence.

Defensive scheme change within and across games, using inferred labels: 99.0% of units show a change, and transition matrices are near-uniform. The record says inferred labels cannot separate real defensive adjustment from the offense executing differently, which is consistent with label noise.
Adapt-vs-continue matched-pair test of the overall-offense H1->H2 excess: Group B CI includes 0 (p=0.386, n=255). Group B is a reconstructed post-hoc cohort.
Descriptive play-type mix shifts in H2 by halftime margin, crunch time and post-run. No inferential tests. The OTHER label is noted as noisy and measurement reliability is limited.
Descriptive team AVOID% ranging 50.6% to 6.8%. No outcome test. Player samples are small (10-178 possessions) and there is no outcome validation.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Predicting H2 suppression from H1 play-type usage without strong mean-reversion control
failed_approaches.why: The apparent suppression was mostly RTM. Matched effects did not survive BH adjustment (limited by selection/regression to the mean).

failed_approaches.what_failed: Explaining H1->H2 PPP collapse with process, usage, lineup and context features
failed_approaches.why: The residual is mostly idiosyncratic small-sample noise. Features added about 1.7 pp beyond RTM.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Using inferred labels to measure defensive scheme change
failed_approaches.why: Label error. Defensive adjustment cannot be separated from offensive execution.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Post-hoc cohort contrasts of adapt vs continue
failed_approaches.why: Placebo dependence and small sample. The cohort is reconstructed, not validated.

evidence_establishes: At game or half level, most H1->H2 change in efficiency is regression to the mean (FAM:SF-APPS-070, FAM:SF-APPS-076, both recorded as rejected).
Observable process, usage, lineup and context features add almost nothing beyond H1 level (FAM:SF-APPS-076).
Inferred defensive-scheme labels are too noisy to support adjustment claims (FAM:SF-APPA-005).
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether a team-level defensive effect on opponents' H2-H1 change is stable across games or seasons. No retrieved record tests team-level reliability of this quantity.
Whether the 65% unexplained variance contains any persistent team component. The record attributes it to noise but does not test it.
Anything about score-based (rather than PPP or play-type-based) H2-H1 change at team-season level.
own_inferences: Because per-game H2-H1 noise is large and RTM dominates, a persistent team component is likely small, so reliability is probably low (my judgment, not a record).
The question is directly testable without inferred labels, using only scoreboard/possession-level H1 and H2 opponent points, which avoids the failure in FAM:SF-APPA-005.
The only way to have a defensible test is to residualize the opponent's H2-H1 change on its own H1 level and expected level, then test persistence of the team-level residual.
A significant raw split-half correlation could be an artifact if H1 defensive quality, pace or conditioning persist and interact mechanically with RTM.
uncertainties: The true between-team SD of the trait is unknown, so power depends on an unobserved quantity.
Whether the 120 units include playoffs. Playoff team-seasons are few and selected, so the main analysis should use the regular season.
Garbage time, rest and tank effects on H2 are not handled in prior records.
Per-game score-state and fouling effects may differ by era and rule changes across 2022-26.

historical_effect.explanation: Prior rejected families (FAM:SF-APPS-070, FAM:SF-APPS-076) show RTM dominates H1->H2 change. I therefore require explicit RTM residualization, a baseline with only H1 level, and a placebo (permuted team labels). Records with label-noise failures (FAM:SF-APPA-005) led me to avoid inferred labels and use raw scoring. Without the records I would have proposed a naive split-half correlation.

blocking_constraints.text: Only 120 team-seasons (about 90 consecutive-season pairs). Year-to-year correlations below about 0.29 cannot be detected at 80% power, and a small real trait would be indistinguishable from zero.
Per-game H2-H1 change is very noisy relative to any plausible team signal, so reliability may be capped near zero regardless of the truth.

prior_work.summary: Earlier work shows that H1->H2 efficiency change is mostly RTM and that observable covariates add little. This is indirect evidence against strong team traits. No retrieved record directly measures the split-half or cross-season reliability of a defense's effect on opponent H2-H1 change.

risks.text: Opponent H2-H1 change is negatively tied to H1 level. Strong defenses depress opponent H1, which mechanically inflates their H2-H1 change. Raw team means confound defensive quality with RTM.
H2-H1 change is a difference of two noisy halves with a built-in negative H1 dependence. Reliability can come from a persistent H1 level rather than from adjustment.
Low signal-to-noise per game. The split-half estimate must be Spearman-Brown corrected and compared with a permutation null.
Opponent offensive quality, schedule, home/away, rest, score state, garbage time, pace and own-team offense can influence H2 opponent scoring.
120 team-seasons gives low power for cross-season persistence.
Rosters, coaches and rules change across seasons, which attenuates year-to-year stability even if a trait exists within season.
Several outcome metrics (points, PPP, eFG) and windows can inflate false positives. One primary metric must be pre-specified.
Inferred scheme labels were noisy in prior work (FAM:SF-APPA-005); do not use them in the primary analysis.

design.estimand: Team-level persistent component of defensive effect on opponents' H2-H1 change: the variance of team random effects (and its reliability) in opponent H2 points per 100 possessions minus H1 points per 100 possessions, after adjusting for the opponent's expected H1 level and RTM.
design.unit: Defense team-season (primary), built from team-games; reliability assessed through split-halves of games within a season and across consecutive seasons.
design.sample: Regular-season games 2022-23 through 2025-26, 30 teams x 4 seasons = 120 team-seasons (about 90 consecutive pairs). Exclude overtime periods from H2, and drop possessions after the score margin exceeds 20 in H2 (garbage time) in the primary analysis, with sensitivity including them. Playoffs are secondary and descriptive only.
design.power: With 90 season pairs, 80% power detects r>=0.29 at alpha 0.05 (two-sided). With 120 team-seasons in the odd/even split-half, r>=0.25 is detectable. Pre-compute the expected reliability from the per-game SD of H2-H1 change (roughly 10 or more points) and the observed team variance; if the estimated signal-to-noise implies reliability under 0.1, report as unresolvable rather than null.
design.controls: Primary model: game-level mixed model of opponent H2-H1 change with covariates: opponent H1 points per 100 (RTM term, plus quadratic), opponent season offensive rating, own defensive rating, home/away, rest days, pace, and the H1 margin at halftime, with random intercepts for defense team-season and opponent. Team trait = the random-effect estimate, with split-half estimated from odd/even games via a Spearman-Brown correction and year-to-year from consecutive seasons using shrunken estimates. Baseline model: H1 level only (replicating FAM:SF-APPS-070 style mean-reversion baselines).
design.falsification: (1) Permute defense team labels within season (1000 permutations) to build a null reliability distribution. (2) Placebo: the same analysis for a quantity with no adjustment story, such as H2-H1 change in the defense's own scoring from the same games or a random-split game halves analog (Q1+Q2 vs Q3+Q4 alternatives such as Q1/Q3 vs Q2/Q4). (3) Negative control: confirm that with the RTM term omitted the raw split-half is inflated, which shows the artifact path. Any reliability that vanishes after RTM adjustment is classed as artifact.
design.multiplicity: One primary metric (opponent points per 100 possessions H2-H1) and one primary reliability estimate (year-to-year r of random-effect estimates). Secondary metrics (eFG%, turnover rate, PPP) are reported with Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment at 0.05.
design.decision_rule: Supported: year-to-year r>=0.30 with lower 95% CI above 0.10 and split-half Spearman-Brown reliability >=0.40, both beating the permutation null at p<0.05 and surviving RTM adjustment, with a placebo r under 0.15. Rejected: the upper 95% CI bound for year-to-year r is below 0.25 and the split-half reliability CI upper bound is below 0.30. Otherwise inconclusive. Artifact if reliability disappears under the RTM-adjusted model.
design.data_version: NBA stats API per-game play-by-play and box-score files, 2022-23 to 2025-26 regular seasons (2025-26 complete as of 2026-04-13), snapshot as of 2026-10-06; freeze the analysis code and the data hash before looking at outcomes.

research_concepts: defensive suppression of opponent second-half change
methodological_questions: Is the defense effect on opponents' H2-H1 change stable across seasons (split-half or year-to-year reliability)?
How much between-team variance remains after regression to the mean and sampling noise with 120 team-seasons?
How should opponent quality, score state, and garbage time be controlled when measuring H2-H1 change?
Is there a mechanical floor or selection effect in H2-H1 change tied to first-half scoring level?
args.query: defense effect on opponents' second-half minus first-half change as a reliable team trait; year-to-year and split-half reliability

system_prompt:
You are a basketball analytics researcher deciding whether and how a research question should be studied.
You work only from the task statement and the tools listed below. Do not assume facts you have not seen.

The work has two stages, in this order.
Stage 1, retrieval:
1. Read the research objective and the data description.
2. Identify the research concepts and methodological questions the task raises.
3. Retrieve historical evidence by calling retrieve_history.
In stage 1 do not assess the question, predict outcomes or decide. Your only stage-1 reply is the retrieve_history call.
Stage 2, assessment, after the retrieval result is returned:
4. Summarise the relevant historical findings and failed approaches.
5. State what the historical evidence does and does not establish.
6. Assess whether the research question is testable.
7. Identify methodological risks and potential confounders.
8. Make the final research decision.
9. Explain whether and how the historical evidence changed the decision.
The stage-2 output format is given together with the retrieval result.

Evidence rules: keep what a retrieved record states (historical_evidence and failed_approaches, each citing the
identifier of a returned record and its status exactly as recorded) separate from your own inference and from
uncertainty or missing information. Cite only identifiers returned by a tool, and never describe an earlier study that
no tool returned. In some settings retrieval returns no records; then state that no historical evidence was available.

Tools:
- retrieve_history(research_concepts, methodological_questions, query): the prescribed retrieval step. Returns the most relevant consolidated study-family records of earlier research by this project that are available in this setting, with their identifiers; returns an empty list when none are available.
- glossary(): definitions of basketball and project terms used in task statements.
- data_catalog(): the fields available in each per-game data file.
- search_documents(query): rank further study-family documents by text relevance; returns up to 10 families not yet returned.
- read_family(id): the complete record of one study family (for example 'FAM:SF-APPA-001').

Protocol: every reply is exactly one JSON object and nothing else.
To call a tool: {"action": "tool", "tool": "<name>", "args": {...}}
To finish (stage 2 only): {"action": "final", "output": <object following the stage-2 schema>}
You may call at most 12 tools; then you must finish. Check that every opening brace has a closing brace.

Risk codes (use only these): SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER, EXPOSURE_SPARSITY, MEASURE_RELIABILITY, RTM_SELECTION, OUTCOME_DERIVED_LABEL, LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD, MECHANICAL_FLOOR, BASE_RATE, CONFOUNDING, LABEL_ERROR, PLACEBO_DEPENDENCE, MULTIPLE_TESTING, IMPLEMENTATION_BUG, DRIFT_NONSTATIONARITY

Research question (as posed on 2026-10-06, in the area of defensive suppression and counter strategy (best/avoid)):
A defense's effect on opponents' H2-H1 change is a reliable team trait.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.
- Units available to a study of this question (as recorded): 120 team-seasons

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

Stage 1. Reply only with the retrieval call: {"action": "tool", "tool": "retrieve_history", "args": {"research_concepts": ["..."], "methodological_questions": ["..."], "query": "..."}}

reasoning_details.text:
I'm weighing whether another tool call is worth it, since I could pull the full text of FAM:SF-APPS-070, but I'll keep things efficient and may just finalize. I need to cite only records I actually got back. The core question is how reliable the defense's effect on opponents' second-half-minus-first-half change is as a stable team trait, across 120 team-seasons.

I'm now working through the design for judging how stable the defense's effect is: split-half and year-to-year checks on a team-level defensive residual, adjusted for opponent's first-half level and quality. With about 120 team-seasons and a small true team-level spread, reliability looks low, so I expect the stability claim to come out weak or unsupported. The regression-to-the-mean pull and the garbage-time and starter-rest effects also have to be removed before any of this can be read.

I'm settling on proceeding with the changes and putting rough odds on the outcomes: supported at about 15%, rejected 35%, untestable 5%, artifact 15%, and uncertain 30%. I've noted the status of each prior record, and the ones I retrieved mostly address play types rather than the reliability of a team defensive trait. Since only 16 teams make the playoffs, I'll use regular-season data for the main analysis, and I'm sketching out the power calculation for detecting a correlation around 0.3 with 90 season pairs.

I'm setting the decision rule for stability: a year-to-year correlation of at least 0.30 whose lower confidence bound stays above 0.15, a split-half Spearman-Brown reliability of at least 0.4, and a result that beats the permutation null. I'll treat it as rejected if the upper confidence bound falls below 0.25.
